title: Timeouts, Retries and Backpressure
summary: Keep a slow dependency from consuming your entire service, and avoid turning retries into an outage amplifier.
body:
A timeout means the caller stopped waiting. It does not prove that the remote operation failed or that its side effect did not happen. Reliability starts by separating these facts. In interviews, this topic surfaces whenever a design calls a slow or flaky dependency (a payment provider, an email service, a database under load) and the interviewer asks "what happens when it slows down?". The answer should cover deadlines, retry policy, bounded queues and isolation, in that order.

## Budget the whole request

Suppose a user request has a two-second deadline. Giving three sequential dependencies two seconds each does not respect that deadline. Propagate a remaining budget, reserve time to return a useful response and cancel work that no longer has a consumer where cancellation is supported. Cover connection establishment and the response, not just one socket operation.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant API as API (deadline 2000 ms)
    participant U as User service
    participant P as Pricing service
    C->>API: GET /checkout
    API->>U: get user, deadline 1900 ms left
    U-->>API: ok after 300 ms
    API->>P: get price, deadline 1600 ms left
    Note over P: overloaded, no reply
    API--xP: cancel at 1500 ms, keep 100 ms reserve
    API-->>C: 503 or cached price, within 2000 ms
```

The API starts with a 2,000 ms budget and passes the remaining time to each dependency (gRPC deadlines and many RPC frameworks carry this in request metadata). The user service answers in 300 ms, leaving about 1,600 ms. The pricing service hangs, so the API gives up at its local cutoff while keeping a small reserve to send a response: an error, or a degraded answer such as a cached price if the product allows it. Downstream services that see an expired deadline should stop working on the request instead of finishing work nobody will read.

Choose timeout values from observed latency and the acceptable false-timeout rate. A timeout that is too short creates unnecessary retries; one that is too long ties up connections and memory. A common starting point is slightly above the dependency's p99 or p99.9 latency under normal load. **Hedged requests** (send a second copy to another replica if the first has not answered by the p95) cut tail latency for idempotent reads at the cost of a few percent extra load.

## Retry only recoverable, safe work

A transient connection failure or a temporary overload may justify a retry. Invalid credentials or a malformed request usually do not. If a write might already have succeeded, use the same idempotency key rather than blindly executing a second write.

Use capped exponential backoff with jitter so clients do not all retry at the same instant. A typical "full jitter" schedule waits a random time between 0 and `min(cap, base * 2^attempt)`: with a 100 ms base and a 2 s cap, attempt 1 waits up to 200 ms, attempt 2 up to 400 ms, and so on. Bound both retry count and total time, and honor a useful `Retry-After` response within that budget. Retry at one chosen layer when possible.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    C["Client: 3 attempts"] --> A["Service A: 3 attempts each"]
    A --> B["Service B: 3 attempts each"]
    B --> D[("Database: up to 27 calls")]
```

Each layer independently retries three times, so one client request can become 3 x 3 x 3 = 27 calls to the database, exactly when the database is struggling. That is how a brief slowdown turns into an outage: the retries keep the overloaded component overloaded. Retry at the edge or at the layer closest to the failure, not both, and add a **retry budget** (for example, retries may add at most 10 percent to normal request volume per client) so retries stop when failures become widespread.

## Bound admission and queues

A queue absorbs a burst; it cannot fix a permanent capacity deficit. If arrivals are 1,200 jobs per second and workers complete 1,000, backlog grows by 200 jobs per second. After one minute, the extra 12,000 jobs represent roughly 12 seconds of work even if arrivals stop.

Size concurrency with Little's law: in-flight work equals arrival rate times time in system. A service handling 500 requests per second at 200 ms each needs about 100 concurrent slots; if the dependency slows to 2 seconds, the same traffic needs 1,000 slots, and a pool of 200 threads or connections is exhausted within a fraction of a second. That is the moment to reject, not to queue.

Limit concurrent work and waiting capacity. When full, reject or defer explicitly rather than buffering without a bound. Depending on the contract, that may mean HTTP 429 for a caller quota or 503 for temporary service capacity. Monitor oldest-job age as well as queue length: a small number of very slow jobs can still violate latency goals. For interactive traffic, a short queue processed newest-first can serve more users within their deadline than a long first-in, first-out queue whose head requests have already timed out on the client.

## Isolate a failing dependency

Use separate concurrency pools (bulkheads) when one provider should not exhaust capacity needed by another. A circuit breaker can stop repeated calls to a failing dependency and allow controlled probes later. It does not replace timeouts, retry limits or recovery monitoring.

| Mechanism | Protects against | Typical setting | Pitfall |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Deadline propagation | Work continuing after the caller gave up | Overall budget per user request | Per-hop timeouts that add up past the budget |
| Retries with jittered backoff | Transient faults | 2 to 3 attempts, capped delay | Retry storms across layers; retrying unsafe writes |
| Bounded queue plus load shedding | Sustained overload | Max depth or max age | Unbounded buffers that hide failure until memory runs out |
| Bulkhead (separate pools) | One dependency starving others | Pool per downstream | Pools too small for normal peaks |
| Circuit breaker | Hammering a dependency that is down | Open after error rate threshold, probe after cool-down | Flapping without half-open probes |

## Common interview mistakes

- Saying "we retry three times" without a budget, backoff or idempotency.
- Treating a timeout as a definite failure and issuing a second payment.
- Adding an unbounded queue and calling the system resilient.
- Scaling workers when the real bottleneck is the dependency they call, which only adds load to it.

## How to use it in an interview

For each external call on the critical path, state the timeout, how many retries and where, and what the user sees when it fails (an error, a degraded response or an accepted-for-later job). Use concrete numbers: the end-to-end deadline, the dependency's normal p99 and the concurrency your pools allow. Expect follow-ups such as "the dependency goes from 100 ms to 10 s, what breaks first?" and "how do you avoid a retry storm when it recovers?".

## Interview exercise

An email provider slows from 100 ms to 10 seconds. Your API receives a steady 100 requests per second. Explain where work is durably accepted, how worker concurrency is limited, what happens when the queue is full, and how duplicate emails are handled after an ambiguous timeout. State what you would measure before increasing worker count.

## Further reading

- [Amazon Builders' Library: timeouts, retries and backoff with jitter](https://aws.amazon.com/builders-library/timeouts-retries-and-backoff-with-jitter/) explains why retries can amplify load and why side effects require care.
- [Google SRE book: handling overload](https://sre.google/sre-book/handling-overload/) covers load shedding, retry budgets and client-side throttling.
keyTakeaways: A timeout is an uncertain outcome, not proof that a side effect did not happen.
Use one overall deadline and bound retries, concurrency and waiting capacity.
Backoff with jitter reduces synchronized retry bursts but cannot create missing capacity.
Observe queue age and dependency saturation before scaling workers.
